To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the frequency modulation rate of a harmonic does not influence the perceived category of a vowel, that the rate of frequency modulation is irrelevant to the perception of speech, and that the rate of modulation is not used by the auditory system to group together simultaneous harmonics into a speech category.

(1) a mistuned harmonic makes only a reduced contribution to a vowel’s perceived category; (2) the rate of frequency modulation of a harmonic does not influence the vowel’s perceived quality; and (3) the rate of modulation of a harmonic is not a cue used to group together frequency components into a vowel.

(i) a mistuned harmonic makes no perceptible contribution to a vowel’s perceived category; (ii) the rate of frequency modulation of a mistuned harmonic does not influence its perceived contribution to a vowel; and (iii) the mistuned harmonic’s frequency modulation is coherent with that of remaining harmonics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of frequency modulation in speech perception.
the perceptual grouping of simultaneous frequency components in speech, and the experiments described here are concerned specifically with the role of frequency modulation in grouping.
the perceptual grouping of simultaneous frequency components in the speech signal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perceptual grouping of frequency components is not a necessary prerequisite for phonetic categorization.
there is a lack of any effect on phonemic categorizations of vowel stimuli by the grouping of frequency-modulating components by rate and phase.
there are no effects of grouping on phonemic categorizations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
frequency-modulated components are not used in phonetic perception.
grouping is not a mechanism for categorization of speech, at least in the case of vowels, and that grouping is not necessary for the perceptual integration of speech.

the perceptual grouping of frequency components in speech is determined primarily by the temporal structure of the stimulus, with the frequency modulation coherence of frequency components playing little if any role in the process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the grouping of frequency components into a vowel category does not depend on the rate and phase of frequency modulation.
the perceptual grouping mechanism that underlies the perception of speech categories is not the same as that which is responsible for the perceptual organization of other types of sounds.
the rate or phase of frequency modulation of a harmonic does not affect the perceptual grouping of that harmonic with other harmonics of a complex tone.
